parts.a: Riverside tree roots reach deep into the bank to reach water and anchor against erosion, or prop roots spread into the mud for stability and oxygen, while plateau trees use deep tap roots to reach groundwater in rocky soil.

ideas.t: Valley roots anchor in the bank or mud and get oxygen (prop roots)
Plateau trees have deep tap roots to reach groundwater

questions.q: Why do many savanna animals travel long distances during the dry season?
o: To escape bush fires that regularly sweep through the savanna
To find water and pasture, which become scarce as water sources dry up
To breed with animals from other parts of the savanna
To avoid the extreme cold of the dry season nights
questions.e: Many savanna animals can go for long periods without water, or travel great distances to find it.

questions.q: A scientist discovers a new animal on the Kwahu Plateau. It has large, broad wings, extremely sharp eyesight, and brown-and-gold feathers that match the colour of dry grass. Based on what you have learned about adaptations to plateau environments, describe what this animal probably eats, how it hunts, and what features you would expect in its feet and beak.

parts.a: It is probably a bird of prey like an eagle: it eats small rodents, hunts by soaring on rising warm air and spotting prey from far away, camouflaged by its brown-and-gold feathers; it would have sharp curved talons and a hooked beak.

ideas.t: It eats small rodents (it is a bird of prey)
It soars on rising warm air and spots prey with sharp eyesight
Sharp curved talons and a hooked beak

questions.q: Climate change is causing Ghana's northern plains to become hotter and drier. Predict two ways in which animals currently living on the plain might be affected, and suggest one adaptation that could help an animal survive if conditions become significantly more extreme.

parts.a: Water and pasture would be scarcer, so animals would need to travel further or may die; heat could affect animals that cannot tolerate it. Survival adaptations include heat resistance, going longer without water or being active only in the cooler morning and evening.

ideas.t: Water and pasture become scarcer
Animals may travel further, die or leave
An adaptation such as heat resistance or long periods without water

questions.q: Why do chameleons have independently moving eyes?
o: To change the colour of their eyes to match their surroundings
To look in two different directions at once, providing nearly all-round vision without moving their head
To see ultraviolet light that helps them find food
To detect movement in complete darkness at night
questions.e: Their independently moving eyes allow them to look in two directions at once, giving almost all-round vision without turning their head.

questions.q: A monkey's prehensile tail is best described as:
o: A tail used for balance only, similar to that of a cat
A tail that can grasp branches, acting as a fifth limb for movement through the canopy
A tail that changes colour to signal to other monkeys
A tail used to store energy in the same way a camel stores fat in its hump
questions.e: Monkeys such as the mona monkey and olive colobus have long limbs and a powerful grip — their hands and feet can grasp branches from multiple angles, allowing them to move rapidly through the canopy.

questions.q: Describe two adaptations of chameleons that help them survive in mountain forests.

parts.a: Laterally compressed body and tong-like feet to grip thin branches; independently moving eyes for all-round vision; colour-changing skin for camouflage.

ideas.t: Compressed body and gripping feet for thin branches
Independently moving eyes or colour-changing skin

questions.q: Compare the wing shape of a savanna bird (such as a kestrel) with a forest bird. Explain why each shape is suited to its environment.

parts.a: Plains birds such as kestrels have long pointed wings for speed in open air, while forest birds have rounded wings for manoeuvring through dense vegetation.

ideas.t: Savanna birds have long pointed wings for speed in open air
Forest birds have rounded wings for manoeuvring through dense vegetation

questions.q: The hippopotamus's eyes, ears and nostrils are positioned on top of its head. This adaptation allows it to:
o: See in all directions while running on land
Sense the world while almost completely submerged in water
Hear prey from greater distances than other animals
Detect heat from the sun while resting on the river bank
questions.e: The hippopotamus is perfectly adapted to an aquatic life — its eyes, ears and nostrils are positioned on top of its head so it can sense the world while almost completely submerged.

questions.q: Describe three features of the hippopotamus that make it well suited to valley life.

parts.a: Its eyes, ears and nostrils are on top of its head so it can sense the world while submerged; its thick, nearly hairless skin secretes a red-tinted fluid that acts as sunscreen and antibiotic; it spends days in the water and grazes at night.

ideas.t: Eyes, ears and nostrils on top of the head
Thick skin secreting a fluid that is sunscreen and antibiotic
Lives in the water by day

questions.q: Describe the key adaptations of the crocodile that make it an effective ambush predator in a river valley.

parts.a: Its streamlined body and powerful tail make it a fast swimmer; it can hold its breath and lie submerged and motionless; its eyes and nostrils are raised on its head so it can watch while almost invisible.

ideas.t: Streamlined body and powerful tail for fast swimming
Holds its breath and lies submerged and motionless
Eyes and nostrils raised on the head

questions.q: Describe two ways in which the natural skin of the hippopotamus protects it from environmental hazards.

parts.a: It secretes a red-tinted fluid that acts as a sunscreen and protects against sunburn, and as an antibiotic that protects against infection.

ideas.t: Protects against sunburn (sunscreen)
Protects against infection (antibiotic)

questions.q: Which of the following correctly defines mutualism?
o: An association in which one organism benefits while the other is unaffected
An association in which both organisms benefit from the relationship
An association in which one organism harms the other while gaining benefit
An association in which both organisms are harmed by living together
questions.e: Mutualism: an association between two organisms in which both benefit from the relationship.

questions.q: Ticks feeding on cattle is an example of which type of association?
o: Mutualism
Commensalism
Parasitism
Predation
questions.e: Ticks are a familiar example in Ghana's farming communities.

questions.q: Define mutualism, parasitism and commensalism. Give one Ghanaian example of each.

parts.a: Mutualism: both organisms benefit (bees and flowers). Parasitism: the parasite benefits and the host is harmed (ticks on cattle). Commensalism: one benefits and the other is unaffected (cattle egrets and cattle).

ideas.t: Mutualism: both organisms benefit
Parasitism: the parasite benefits and the host is harmed
Commensalism: one benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed
Examples such as bees and flowers, ticks and cattle, cattle egrets

questions.q: A school science club is studying a forest near their community. They observe: (a) moss growing on the bark of trees, (b) ticks on a deer, and (c) bees visiting wildflowers. Classify each observation as mutualism, parasitism or commensalism, and explain your reasoning for each classification.

parts.a: (a) Moss on tree bark is commensalism: the moss benefits, the tree is unaffected. (b) Ticks on a deer are parasitism: the tick feeds on blood and the deer is harmed. (c) Bees visiting wildflowers are mutualism: the bees get nectar and the flowers are pollinated.

ideas.t: (a) Moss on bark: commensalism (the tree is unaffected)
(b) Ticks on a deer: parasitism (tick feeds, deer harmed)
(c) Bees and wildflowers: mutualism (nectar and pollination)

questions.q: In the relationship between leguminous plants and Rhizobium bacteria, which statement is correct?
o: The bacteria harm the plant by taking nutrients from its roots
The plant harms the bacteria by crowding them out of the soil
Both the bacteria and the plant benefit: bacteria get carbohydrates; the plant gets usable nitrogen
The plant benefits by getting nitrogen while the bacteria are unaffected
questions.e: Another important example in Ghanaian farming communities is the relationship between leguminous plants (such as cowpeas, groundnuts and soybeans) and nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

questions.q: Which of the following associations would have the most severe consequences if the beneficial partner were removed from an ecosystem?
o: Commensalism between a cattle egret and cattle
Mutualism between bees and flowering plants, because removing bees disrupts pollination of most food crops
Parasitism between ticks and cattle, because the ticks control cattle populations
Commensalism between epiphytic orchids and forest trees
questions.e: Mutualism creates networks of interdependence — remove the bees from a forest and the flowering plants cannot reproduce, leading to collapse of the whole food web above them.

questions.q: Explain the mutualistic relationship between leguminous plants and Rhizobium bacteria. Why is this relationship important for Ghanaian farmers?

parts.a: Rhizobium bacteria live in nodules on the roots of legumes and change nitrogen gas from the air into a form the plant can use; the plant gives the bacteria carbohydrates. Farmers benefit because legumes improve the soil for later crops.

ideas.t: Rhizobium bacteria live in nodules on legume roots
They convert nitrogen from the air into a form the plant can use
The plant gives them carbohydrates
Legumes improve the soil for later crops

questions.q: Describe the relationship between bees and flowering plants. Which type of association is this and why?

parts.a: It is mutualism. Bees collect nectar for food and carry pollen from flower to flower, enabling fertilisation, so both benefit.

ideas.t: Mutualism
The bee gets nectar (food)
The plant gets its pollen transferred, so it can reproduce

questions.q: A farmer in the Upper East Region notices that her cowpeas (a leguminous plant) are growing much better than her maize on the same farm. After the cowpea harvest, the soil where they grew produces healthier maize the following season. Using your knowledge of associations, explain what happened in the soil under the cowpeas, and recommend how she could use this knowledge to improve all her crops.

parts.a: Cowpeas are legumes with Rhizobium bacteria in their root nodules, which change nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use, enriching the soil. She should grow legumes in rotation with maize and other crops to improve the soil.

ideas.t: Rhizobium bacteria in cowpea root nodules
They convert nitrogen from the air into a usable form, improving the soil
Recommend planting legumes before or alongside other crops (rotation)

questions.q: In the oxpecker-cattle relationship, what benefit does the cattle receive?
o: Nutrients from the food that the oxpecker shares
Removal of ticks and parasites from its skin, and warning signals when the bird takes flight
Protection from predators who fear the oxpecker
Grooming of its fur that improves insulation in cold weather
questions.e: The animal gets relief from irritating parasites and a warning signal when the bird takes flight.

questions.q: Why do most parasites NOT immediately kill their hosts?
o: Parasites cannot harm organisms that are larger than themselves
A living host provides ongoing benefits to the parasite; a dead host is useless
Parasites are too small to cause enough harm to kill a large host
Most parasites form a mutualistic relationship with the host over time
questions.e: Importantly, most parasites do not immediately kill their hosts, because a dead host provides no further benefit.

questions.q: The Striga plant is a devastating agricultural parasite in northern Ghana because it:
o: Produces toxins that poison the soil and kill nearby plants
Attaches its roots to cereal crop roots and withdraws water, nutrients and carbohydrates
Spreads rapidly by producing thousands of seeds that germinate in the rainy season
Shades out crops by growing taller than them and blocking their sunlight
questions.e: Striga attaches its roots to the roots of cereal crops such as maize, sorghum and millet.

questions.q: Explain how the Striga plant is a parasite of cereal crops. Describe the harm it causes to maize plants in Ghana.

parts.a: Striga (witchweed) attaches its roots to the roots of maize, sorghum and millet and withdraws water, nutrients and carbohydrates, reducing maize yields by 40 to 80 percent in heavily infested fields.

ideas.t: It attaches its roots to the roots of cereal crops
It withdraws water, nutrients and carbohydrates
It reduces yields by 40 to 80 percent

questions.q: Explain why parasites do not usually kill their hosts immediately. What would happen to the parasite if the host died?

parts.a: A living host keeps providing food for the parasite, but a dead host provides no further benefit, so the parasite would also lose its food and home.

ideas.t: A living host keeps providing benefit
A dead host is useless to the parasite

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of commensalism?
o: Bees collecting nectar and pollinating flowers in return
Ticks feeding on cattle blood and causing anaemia
Cattle egrets catching insects disturbed by grazing cattle, without affecting the cattle
Rhizobium bacteria providing nitrogen to leguminous plants in exchange for carbohydrates
questions.e: The bird catches the insects disturbed by the plough; the farmer is neither helped nor harmed.

questions.q: Malaria is caused by a parasitic organism called Plasmodium. Which statement about this parasite is correct?
o: Plasmodium is a virus that is carried by the Aedes mosquito
Plasmodium is a parasitic organism carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes that lives and reproduces inside human red blood cells
Plasmodium is a bacterial parasite transmitted by drinking contaminated water
Plasmodium is a fungal parasite that infects only animals, not humans
questions.e: Malaria is caused by a parasitic organism — Plasmodium — carried by the female Anopheles mosquito.

questions.q: Epiphytic orchids growing on tree branches in a forest hill are an example of commensalism because:
o: They steal nutrients from the tree's vascular system while giving nothing in return
The tree provides them with nutrients and water through the bark
They use the tree's height and structure to access light without taking anything from the tree
They pollinate the tree's flowers in return for using the tree's surface
questions.e: These epiphytes use the tree's height and structure to gain access to light, but they do not take nutrients from the tree's vascular system.

questions.q: Describe the cattle egret-cattle relationship and explain why it is classified as commensalism rather than mutualism.

parts.a: Cattle egrets follow cattle and catch grasshoppers and frogs disturbed by the cattle. The egret benefits but the cattle are neither helped nor harmed, so it is commensalism, not mutualism.

ideas.t: Egrets follow cattle and catch insects and frogs they disturb
The cattle are unaffected
So it is commensalism because only one benefits

questions.q: What is Plasmodium and how does it harm its human host? What organism carries it?

parts.a: Plasmodium is a parasitic organism that causes malaria. It lives and reproduces in the human body and causes fever and organ damage, and can kill. It is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito.

ideas.t: A parasitic organism that causes malaria
It causes fever and organ damage and can kill
Carried by the female Anopheles mosquito

questions.q: Describe the relationship between epiphytic orchids and forest trees. Is this mutualism, parasitism or commensalism? Explain your classification.

parts.a: It is commensalism. The orchid uses the tree's height and structure to reach light but takes no nutrients from the tree, so the orchid benefits and the tree is unaffected.

ideas.t: Commensalism
The orchid benefits by using the tree's height to get light
The tree is unaffected because nothing is taken from it

questions.q: Which of the following explains why mutualistic associations are important for ecosystem stability?
o: They reduce the number of organisms in an ecosystem, making it more manageable
They create networks of interdependence; removing one partner can cause the collapse of systems that depend on it
They make organisms more competitive, leading to the survival of the strongest
They replace parasitic relationships and prevent harmful associations from developing
questions.e: Mutualism creates networks of interdependence — remove the bees from a forest and the flowering plants cannot reproduce, leading to collapse of the whole food web above them.

questions.q: Why is the Striga plant particularly damaging in northern Ghana's farms?
o: It directly attacks the farmer rather than the crops
It was introduced from Europe where maize varieties had evolved resistance to it; Ghanaian varieties had not
Local maize varieties have no evolved resistance to Striga's parasitic strategy, and soil degradation has increased its spread
It only grows during the dry season when farmers cannot remove it
questions.e: The Striga weed — believed to have increased in northern Ghana due to soil degradation — is devastating because local maize varieties were not evolved to resist its particular parasitic strategy.

questions.q: Explain why mutualistic associations are critical to the functioning of ecosystems. Use the example of pollinators and flowering plants.

parts.a: Mutualism creates networks of interdependence. If the pollinators such as bees are removed, flowering plants cannot reproduce and the whole food web above them can collapse.

ideas.t: Mutualism creates networks of interdependence
If bees are removed, flowering plants cannot reproduce
The whole food web can collapse

questions.q: Explain how parasitism can sometimes have an indirect positive effect on a population, even though it harms individual hosts.

parts.a: Parasites often affect sick or weak individuals most, which indirectly improves the overall health of the host population and keeps populations in check.

ideas.t: Parasites preferentially affect sick or weak individuals
So the overall health of the host population improves

questions.q: Describe how the introduction of an invasive parasite into an ecosystem where organisms have no evolved resistance can be devastating. Use a specific Ghanaian example.

parts.a: Organisms with no evolved resistance suffer catastrophic damage. Striga weed in northern Ghana is devastating because local maize varieties are not evolved to resist it, and its spread has increased with soil degradation.

ideas.t: Organisms have no evolved resistance, so the damage is catastrophic
Example: the Striga weed in northern Ghana
Local maize varieties are not resistant
